headline: Saudi WoodShow Opens in Riyadh With Timber and Woodworking Machinery
deck: The third edition of the Saudi International Wood and Woodworking Machinery Show runs from 1 to 3 September, adding a manufacturing show to a week already dominated by construction.
excerpt: The third Saudi WoodShow has opened at the Riyadh International Convention and Exhibition Center, running from 1 to 3 September under the patronage of the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources. It covers timber, woodworking machinery, production technology and furniture components, and lands in the same week as Big 5 Construct Saudi.
content:
The third edition of the Saudi International Wood and Woodworking Machinery Show, Saudi WoodShow, has opened at the Riyadh International Convention and Exhibition Center, running from 1 to 3 September. The exhibition is held under the patronage of the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources, with the Riyadh Chamber as strategic partner, and brings together suppliers of timber, woodworking machinery, production technologies and furniture components.

Exhibitors are drawn from Saudi Arabia, Portugal, France, the United States, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates and China, a spread that reflects where the Kingdom currently buys most of its wood products and most of the equipment used to process them. The show positions itself as a sourcing and manufacturing event rather than a trade fair for finished furniture, which is the more commercially interesting framing: the machinery hall is where a decision to import a finished product turns into a decision to make one locally.

That distinction matters because wood is one of the more import-dependent parts of the Saudi building materials chain. Structural steel, cement, concrete, pipe and cable all have substantial domestic production behind them. Panels, engineered boards, sawn timber and joinery components largely do not, and they arrive in a market where fit-out demand is being generated at scale by hotels, housing, retail and the interiors packages of the giga-projects. The distribution layer that serves that demand is well established — Masdar, the Al-Muhaidib building materials business founded in 1971, operates more than a hundred branches across the Kingdom and stocks timber, wooden sheets and decorative panels alongside steel and plumbing — but distribution is not the same as production.

The Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources has been consistent about where it wants that to go. The Kingdom passed 12,000 factories by the end of 2024 and has set a target of 36,000 by 2035, and the industrial strategy has repeatedly identified downstream, lower-capital manufacturing as the segment where new licences convert most quickly into output. Woodworking sits in exactly that band: the machinery is affordable relative to a steel mill or a chemicals plant, the skills are transferable, and the customer is a domestic construction sector already ordering the finished article from abroad.

Procurement policy is moving in the same direction. The Local Content and Government Procurement Authority has been phasing in minimum local content percentages for products on the mandatory list used by government buyers, and the Made in Saudi programme requires added value of at least 40 percent, or main components sourced entirely within the Kingdom, for a product to carry the label. Neither instrument creates a wood industry by itself. Both change the arithmetic for a manufacturer weighing whether to ship finished goods into Riyadh or to assemble them there.

The timing is not accidental. Saudi WoodShow opens while Big 5 Construct Saudi is still running at Riyadh Front, giving the city two industrial exhibitions in the same week with overlapping visitor bases — contractors, fit-out specialists, developers and distributors who buy structural materials and interior materials from the same budget. The wood sector's own bridge into that crowd was on display at Big 5, where the circular-economy strand of the show recognised carbon-negative wood-based panels and engineered boards distributed in the Kingdom by Masdar under the Kronospan brand.

For visitors, the practical value of the machinery halls is the same as the practical value of the equipment halls across town: a chance to see production lines, cutting and edge-banding equipment, finishing systems and material handling in one place, and to work out what a small Saudi plant would actually need to run. The Kingdom's furniture and joinery demand is not in question. Whether it is met by containers or by factories is what the next few editions of this show will record.
author: BrentDesk Staff
